sources.title: The Journey of Crimson Desert Continues with Charting the Unknown
sources.text: Since its launch in March, the world of Crimson Desert — where Kliff and the Greymanes fight to rebuild what they lost — has grown with each update. Alongside improvements, the game has received brand new content, including boss rematches, and new features shaped by players’ adventures and stories across Pywel. In August, we released Patch Version 2.00. The free update added new story moments and expanded voice-over and language support. Together with all the post-launch updates up to that date, the update came out as Crimson Desert Enhanced . Lastly, with the launch of Charting the Unknown on October 29, Pywel is growing once again with even more adventures. The DLC brings new journeys across land and, for the first time, at sea, along with new ways to enrich your life in Pywel. Charting the Unknown is available now on XBOX Series X|S. We want to thank all our Greymanes out there for the incredible support they have shown for Crimson Desert since launch. Your love for the game has brought us this far, and we are excited for you to experience what the DLC has to offer. Now, let’s take a look at what awaits you in Charting the Unknown. Charting the Unknown introduces three new storylines, one each for Kliff, Oongka, and Damiane. With the fight for the Greymanes and Pywel behind them, each character sets out to forge their own path. Along the way, they will meet allies and threats both old and new, and chart their own course forward. The DLC brings something many players have been asking for: ocean exploration. Dive into the sea and explore the underwater world, where you will discover ruins, treasure chests, and new creatures and mounts. You can also build your own ship and set sail across the Great Ocean of Pywel. Charting the Unknown also deepens life in the world. Kliff, Oongka, and Damiane can form deeper bonds with some of Pywel’s inhabitants. Interact with them to build trust and strengthen your relationship, which may eventually blossom into romance and even marriage. An upgraded housing system now lets you build your house from the ground up. And from the layout of the interior to the placement of walls, windows, and other structural elements, you have more control than ever to design your home, sweet home. There’s more: select castles, once liberated, can become yours. This will allow you to decorate their courtyards and interiors with unique objects and furnishings, turning a hard-won stronghold into another place you can call your own. Also, if you want to take a more active role in the strongholds you have liberated, you can lease certain facilities such as a restaurant or a smithy and run them yourself. Assign equipment and comrades, decide which goods to sell, and grow each location’s recognition. For those who don’t always like life too peaceful, Charting the Unknown has new content for you. The Garden of Trials is a combat-focused challenge where you face the bosses you have met throughout your adventures in Pywel, one after another. So test your skills and mettle to see if you hold up against these formidable foes. Whether you are a seasoned Greymane or just taking your first steps in Pywel, there is plenty to discover. And if you have not set out on the journey yet, this is the perfect time to do so! Crimson Desert is offering a 5-hour free trial of the base game for XBOX players from October 29 through January 6, so take the opportunity to step into Pywel and reach beyond!

sources.title: Crimson Desert: Charting the Unknown Review So Far
sources.text: Crimson Desert’s biggest strength is in the sheer volume of stuff it throws at you, allowing you to spend hundreds or even a thousand-plus hours doing everything from hunting animals with a bow to developing a gambling addiction at the tavern. So it’s not very surprising that Crimson Desert’s first paid DLC, called Charting the Unknown, prioritizes adding more on top of its already staggeringly large repertoire. So far, the interesting new activities that mostly focus on oceanic adventures are exactly as compelling as you’d hope, with ship-to-ship combat, underwater exploration, and romance options being among the list of new worthwhile features. On the other hand, existing activities that have added content, like the extra story missions, have mostly been uninspired retreads that don’t do anything to improve upon their established shortcomings. When Crimson Desert came out, I said that its content was a mile long and an inch deep, and for better or worse this DLC seems to say, “Here’s another half-mile.” The most disappointing part of the DLC so far has been the additional story missions, which are only accessible once you’ve completed the base game’s already dense main story (a feat which only 10% of Steam players have done, judging by the achievements system). At least the handful of missions I’ve completed at this point have mostly served as an expanded epilogue of sorts, with Kliff fighting more difficult versions of old bosses from the existing story, and Damiane and Oongka fleshing out their less substantial stories as well. I’m not far enough to know if any of these quests eventually become more interesting, but most of their objectives have been an oddly bland retracing of your steps, like going back to spend time with a familiar character and share a moment fishing together or arm wrestle someone to gather information as an apparent callback to an identical moment in the original story. I did get to a new stretch of the map just before getting distracted by the separate seafaring content, so hopefully this part of the DLC will pick up the pace, but so far it’s been about as unimpressive as I expected given the low bar for storytelling in Crimson Desert. Much like the base content though, most of the effort seems to have been put into things that aren’t related to the story. Although most of my time has been spent dipping my toes into the water-based ship-crafting feature that’s the focus of this expansion, it feels like I’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg, with new resources to obtain, crewmates to hire, and even more activities to learn like harpooning fish and ship-to-ship combat before you can really begin your voyages properly. It's going to take more time to fully engage with these new activities and judge whether or not they have the sea legs to keep me entertained for longer than a few hours, but at least right now I’m just impressed (yet again) by the fact that these systems exist in this adventure that’s already so damn packed with things to do. Gliding underwater on the back of a sea turtle and captaining your own pirate crew truly just feel completely bizarre in the context of Crimson Desert, and so far that’s been compelling enough to keep me moving forward even if some of the other added content isn’t great. There’s still a ton I have to investigate, like additional base building and property management features, a challenging combat arena-style gauntlet, and my personal favorite – social links and romance mechanics for NPCs, which I’m very excited to check out once I’ve gotten my bearings (I’m just not ready to settle down yet, okay?!). For all the stuff that’s been added, one thing that is the same since the last time I played is the number of bugs I’ve encountered in my brief time with the Charting the Unknown DLC. I’ve already had two hard crashes, one character wig out on me while I was trying to arm wrestle him (he was hilariously standing behind me during the match, arm bent unnaturally), and quite a few blurry or flickering textures that are impossible for me to not focus on during cutscenes. I’m still too early to tell if this is going to be a consistent issue, but in my time so far it’s been quite rocky from a technical perspective considering how much wonkiness I’ve encountered per hour played. As expected with Crimson Desert, it’s going to take quite a bit of time to see and do enough to reach a definitive conclusion on Charting the Unknown, and I’m hopeful that the engaging and unexpected content that’s been added will be able to make up for some of the activities that feel like empty calories. Travis Northup is a writer for IGN. You can follow him on Twitter @TieGuyTravis and read his games coverage here .

stories.summary: The MMORPG's next expansion was set to launch shortly after the new year, but Warriors of Light will have to wait a bit longer.

sources.title: Final Fantasy XIV Evercold Delayed, New Release Date Announced at FFXIV Fan Fest
sources.text: Final Fantasy XIV Evercold was set to launch sometime in January 2027, which was announced as part of its initial reveal back in April this year during the North American FFXIV Fan Fest. However, this next expansion for the critically acclaimed MMORPG has been delayed – FFXIV Evercold's release date is now February 23, 2027 (and February 19, 2027 for early access). This was announced alongside the new, full trailer / intro cinematic for Evercold at FFXIV Fan Fest in Japan, and was said to only be a four-week delay. In typical FFXIV fashion, the third and final teaser trailer is the full opening cinematic for an expansion, and it kicked off the Japan Fan Fest keynote where director and producer Naoki Yoshida presented more details on new features, where the ongoing story is headed, and fundemental gameplay changes as FFXIV goes into version 8.0 alongside Evercold's launch. Pre-orders for Evercold open on November 4, 2026 and will come with a Wind-up Kottr minion to summon and follow you around in the world and Halone's Earring which will boost the EXP you gain for Jobs under level 100 when equipped. The collector's edition comes with the Valhallar Odin mount, the Entreat Crystal emote, and the Crystal Skyltborg which looks like glam for the new Bastion Job's weapons. The physical collector's bundle has the Evercold art book, the Tapestry of the Fourth decoration, a Kottr plush, a keychain of the Ethos Metal, and the Warrior of Light Reaper figure. Additionally, we got a glimpse of the second new Job coming to his new expansion. It's a ranged DPS called Zephyr, which rocks a crossbow as their primary weapon and commands an avian companion to provide support. There's a lot coming to FFXIV Evercold in addition to a new world and main story including a Neon Genesis Evangelion crossover raid series (which got a new teaser trailer) , a Final Fantasy VII crossover raid series, a new Tank Job with Bastion, and much more. Be sure to check out my Dawntrail review as well to look back at the last expansion before heading into this new era for FFXIV. sources.title: EA reportedly closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between Mass Effect 5 and Star Wars Battlefront 3
sources.text: And it chose the "less risky, more predictable bet". A new report has revealed that EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter. The revelation comes from Bloomberg , which heard from "people familiar with the company's strategy" that the "recent emergence" of an opportunity to develop a third Battlefront game meant EA - a company saddled with $18bn in debt because of the recent leveraged buyout - would have two sci-fi projects, each likely to cost hundreds of millions of dollars to make. It couldn't afford to make both of them so EA executives chose Star Wars Battlefront 3, because it was seen "as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect", Bloomberg reported - despite development for the game not even having begun yet. An EA spokesperson said the company had "collectively reached this decision following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities". "While this is never easy," the spokesperson went on, "we ultimately have to make tough decisions to focus our teams on the biggest opportunities for our future, including investing in new projects across our portfolio." The report highlights a few other contributing factors in EA's decision, including BioWare's unfavourable recent track record and a reorganisation of its executive ranks to include more EA Sports people, in favour of those advocating for BioWare. EA bosses even lamented Dragon Age: Veilguard's sales, suggesting it would have been better if the title was 'a live service game' . Last week, following the announcement of BioWare's closure and the cancellation of Mass Effect 5 , an internal video for the project - known as Mass Effect Universe - was leaked , showing what appears to be a pre-rendered visualisation of it. The game was said to take place 600 years after the Reaper war, in the midst of a galactic cold war, and to have the player be "a cross between John Wick and James Bond" in terms of what they'd be capable of. There was a promise of "Hitman-style freedom" in approaching levels, romance that "wasn't being sanitised", and for connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. It's not clear how much work was done on it, but clearly a lot of planning had been done - far more, certainly, than has been done on Battlefront 3. EA's Star Wars Battlefront 2 was released in 2017 and struggled, initially, to convince - partly because it was riddled with loot boxes. But years of adjustments and improvements left it in a much better place.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: There are currently "no other Assassin's Creed remakes actively in development", says Ubisoft
sources.text: Yesterday, Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, and the publisher's comments included quite a big surprise: there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works. "One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin’s Creed remake actively in development," Ubisoft said in a statement on its website . "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories." This has come as a shock to some players because, back in 2024, Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot specifically mentioned that upcoming remakes - plural - were in active development across Ubisoft studios. "Firstly, players can be excited about some remakes, which will allow us to revisit some of the games we've created in the past and modernise them; there are worlds in some of our older Assassin's Creed games that are still extremely rich," Guillemot said. Given the success of this year's Black Flag Resynced - which sold over 3.5 million copies and "exceeded annual expectations within its first 14 days" - it's interesting to hear Ubisoft move away from what clearly seemed a popular way of revisiting older games. But it's worth noting that although Ubisoft isn't currently working on remakes, that doesn't mean we won't get them at some point in the future. "Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back," the company's statement continued. "That door remains open because, after all... Nothing is true, everything is permitted." That last bit, if you're unfamiliar, is a commonly-repeated motto amongst the Assassin Order. If you're curious about what's next for the franchise, we've got a few ideas. First, there's ' Codename Invictus ', which is billed as a "PvP multiplayer Assassin's Creed experience" being led by a team of For Honor veterans at Ubisoft Montreal. The title remains shrouded in mystery, and we've seen nothing of how the game will look or play yet. Then there's Assassin's Creed Hexe, in development at Ubisoft Montreal. This game is touted as a "darker, narrative-driven" experience that appeared to be aiming for a 16th century European setting when it was announced back in 2022 . It was originally believed to be targeting a 2026 release, but earlier this year , Ubisoft head of franchise Jean Guesdon explained the publisher is "taking the time to deliver on its ambitious vision, which means we'll be quiet for a little longer". Following this, a report emerged in August stating that Hexe is still at least a year away . The Assassin's Creed series remains a pillar of Ubisoft's output, even if the publisher has been enduring a lot of change lately. Late last year, the leader of the Assassin's Creed franchise, Marc-Alexis Côté, left Ubisoft. This coincided with a reorganisation of the company and the creation of the Vantage Studios subsidiary, established by Ubisoft and Tencent, to oversee development of the French publisher's biggest franchises , which includes Assassin's Creed.

sources.title: Ubisoft says no more Assassin’s Creed remakes are planned, as it gives updates on Invictus and Hexe
sources.text: Black Flag Resynced will be the only remade Assassin’s Creed for now Ubisoft has given an update on its Assassin’s Creed games in development, and has stressed that a remake isn’t one of them. In a Fall 2026 update posted on the official Ubisoft website, head of content Jean Guesdon gave an update on the progress of its multiplayer Assassin’s Creed game codenamed Invictus, as well as its darker, horror-based Assassin’s Creed codenamed Hexe. Guesdon also addressed player speculation about more remakes, following the success of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, and stressed that none are currently in development. “As our first-ever franchise remake, Resynced taught us a tremendous amount,” he explained. “Taking on a game that holds such a special place in players’ hearts brought both excitement and challenges. “Rebuilding old systems from scratch, adding new elements that fit the experience, and balancing legacy with innovation was a massive undertaking. We’re super proud of what the Resynced team delivered and how well it was received. “One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin’s Creed remake actively in development. Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin’s Creed titles, including projects you haven’t heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories. “But don’t mistake that for a closed door. Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we’ll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back.” Elsewhere in the update, Guesdon gave an update on the Assassin’s Creed multiplayer spin-off codenamed Invictus. He explained that hundreds of players joined the first private Insiders Session a few months ago and played an early prototype, before sharing feedback with the development team. “The response to the return of PVP multiplayer was very positive,” he said. “Insiders particularly enjoyed the parkour and verticality of our maps, the dynamic teamplay, and the chance to play as various Assassin’s Creed characters, each with their own skills and playstyles. “One piece of feedback came through clearly, though â players saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin’s Creed. The team spent the past months acting on it, and Invictus is now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions. “We’re proud of the work so far and very excited for the year ahead. Invictus is still in development, so information you come across online may be incomplete, outdated, or inaccurate. We’ll keep testing new iterations and update you as soon as we have more to share.” As for Assassin’s Creed: Hexe, Ubisoft’s more horror-based take on the series which revolves around witches, Guesdon suggested it may still be a while off, with more information coming next year at some point. “We’re making steady progress on this darker Assassin’s Creed experience, though there is still work ahead of us,” he explained. “We know the wait has been long, and we’re grateful for your patience and continued enthusiasm for the project. “The team remains focused on delivering the unique vision at the heart of this project, and we’ll share our next major update in 2027. Until we’re ready to share more, we’ll keep enjoying your theories, discussions, and excitement as this experience continues to take shape.”

sources.text: Get a taste of Mouthwashing on the big screen Mouthwashing is one of the best horror games in recent years and, now, it's been turned into a movie. As per The Hollywood Reporter , Scott Derrickson – of Sinister, Black Phone and Doctor Strange fame – will be producing the adaptation of the Wrong Organ-developed title, which launched on consoles earlier this week after taking PC by storm. The non-linear narrative and unique visuals helped mark Mouthwashing out as a modern horror classic, with the game taking home the award for Best Narrative at 2024's Horror Game Awards. Mouthwashing is the latest in the trend of horror games being turned into movies. Most notably, Zach Cregger's Resident Evil delivered its own twisted take on Raccoon City in September, but there has also been the likes of Exit 8 and Five Nights at Freddy's ready to scare us silly in recent years. sources.title: Every Resident Evil Game, Ranked From Worst to Best
sources.text: After decades of misses, 2026 gave us one of the best gaming adaptations of all time. Well, sort of. Zach Cregger’s take on Resident Evil was a hit among critics who have praised the horror movie for its delightfully playful tone. The only catch is that it didn't have much to do with the established lore and characters of the actual Resident Evil games . Instead, it told its own story in the universe, which is probably for the better, considering how complicated the game saga gets. If you want to dip into that saga after seeing the movie, though, you have a lot of options. Resident Evil has several entry points across dozens of mainline games and spinoffs. There are only 11 core games to worry about, if you want the bulk of the story without bonus worldbuilding tidbits, but there are some real ups and downs within that list. To help you sort through it all, we’ve put together an updated ranking of the main Resident Evil series, complete with this year’s Resident Evil Requiem . (Note that we’re grouping games and their remakes together as one here, as we’re focused on where those games fit into the Resident Evil story overall.) There are people out there who will argue that Resident Evil 5 is an underrated gem. They will say that there’s more nuance to its story than its lousy reputation would have you think. They will say that despite its problems, it really sings in co-op. To each their own, truly — but I would rather be mauled by zombie dogs than replay Resident Evil 5 . If you’re an advocate for it, I implore you to revisit it to get an updated feel for a torturously clumsy third-person shooter that has aged like raw fish. If I’m being honest, I’d consider myself a Resident Evil 6 apologist. I know that’s a ludicrous thing to say after slamming Resident Evil 5 supporters, but look: Resident Evil 6 actually gets the series’ tone. It takes the B-movie energy of the original games and takes them to the silliest peak possible. It plays terribly and features some storylines that are absolute duds, but Leon’s arc is an underappreciated bit of Resident Evil wackiness that deserves its flowers. Resident Evil 0 has a strong elevator pitch that the game itself doesn’t fully live up to. The prequel begins on a train, completely mixing up — or at least elongating — the puzzle-box nature of the games that came before it. Beyond that memorable setpiece, Resident Evil 0 mostly just functions as a fan-servicing complement to the GameCube’s excellent Resident Evil remake. A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later. Code: Veronica is one of those games whose legacy will likely be defined by its upcoming remake. At the time, it was hailed as a crowning achievement for a series seemingly at its peak. Return to it now and you’ll have to fight through some tough controls to enjoy Claire Redfield’s story. It’s worth pushing through the pain, but expect Resident Evil Veronica to trigger a proper critical reappraisal soon. Depending on how you feel about Resident Evil Village ’s various segments , this one could either rank very high or very low on this list. The dollhouse? One of the finest few hours in the entire series. The Frankenstein factory? Well, not so much. It's an uneven game, but that’s part of Village ’s charm; the amusement park nature of its story makes for an eclectic game that has at least something you’ll adore. Though its 2020 remake didn’t do as much to elevate its stock as 2019’s Resident Evil 2 did for that entry, the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis is still a special game. Its persistently prowling Nemesis gave the series a terrifying calling card that it continues to make good use of. Plus, it’s one of the few games that gives Jill Valentine a chance to shine, and her aura carries both the original and the remake. More time will likely need to pass until we can truly figure out where Resident Evil Requiem stacks up compared to other entries in the series, but as of now, it’s firmly in the top tier. That’s thanks to a strong dual-hero story that balances Grace Ashcroft’s personal nightmare and confronts a wider trauma surrounding the destruction of Raccoon City through Leon S. Kennedy’s eyes. Its ability to seamlessly jump between those two things, while switching from survival horror to pure action, leaves a lot to applaud in a well-executed arc capstone. The Resident Evil series seemed like it was at a dead end in 2017 after a pair of back-to-back stinkers, so Resident Evil 7 was a necessary jolt of life. The sequel’s pivot from action back to straight survival horror made for hands-down the series’ scariest game. The story of Ethan Winters and his war against mold might not be as compelling as the Raccoon City saga, but Resident Evil 7 proved that there were still plenty of new stories that could be told in the zombie-infested world. Whether you play the original PS1 version of Resident Evil or its GameCube remake, you simply can’t sleep on the series’ first entry. That’s not just because it set the stage for all things Resident Evil both narratively and in gameplay, but because it's still the series’ most focused game. The Spencer Mansion remains a perfect puzzle box that’s dripping with atmosphere. The jump scares are terrifying, the bosses are memorable, and it features the best cast of characters ever assembled in a Resident Evil game. Before 2019’s Resident Evil 2 remake , I likely would have given its predecessor the edge here. However, Capcom’s stellar revisit served as a welcome reminder that Leon and Claire’s hellish trip through the Raccoon City Police Department is an all-time great horror story. It successfully widened out the world of Resident Evil while still keeping things intimate and terrifying. It’s one hell of an introduction for Leon too, who makes for a compelling hero as a rookie cop who is immediately in over his head. It’s hard to imagine the series being as big as it is now without his intro

sources.title: Maddy Makes Games removes Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox in support of pro-Palestinian BDS boycott
sources.text: Indie developers join the creators of Luck be a Landlord, Ice Water, and All Will Rise in removing games from Xbox Indie developer Maddy Makes Games has delisted Celeste and TowerFall from Xbox to support the pro-Palestinian Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement. According to GamesRadar , players noticed both games were removed from the platform yesterday. Maddy Thorson later confirmed this on social media . "For those who're asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox," Thorson wrote. "We did this to support the BDS boycott." Maddy Makes Games is among several developers supporting the BDS boycott. Most recently, Big Walk developer House House announced it would not release its co-op game on Xbox. "It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to these intentions," the developer said. "We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets. We've made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free." Other developers supporting the boycott include Ice Water, creator of Tenderfoot Tactics ; Speculative Agency, developer of All Will Rise; and Dan Dilorio, creator of Luck be a Landlord . The BDS boycott was established following concerns that Microsoft's Azure and AI technologies were being used by the Israeli Ministry of Defence (IMOD) "to target civilians or cause harm in the conflict in Gaza," according to an Associated Press investigation. Microsoft acknowledged that it provides the IMOD "with software, professional services, Azure cloud and AI services," but concluded after its own internal review that it has "no evidence to date" that its technology has "been used to target or harm people" in the ongoing conflict.

sources.text: Director of both games, Maddy Thorson, confirmed the intent on BlueSky. Earlier this month, Big Walk developer House House explained why their co-op puzzle adventure wouldn't be available for sale on Xbox : Microsoft's gaming division is a priority target of the the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which names the tech giant in general as a pressure target alongside Google, Amazon, and a host of other companies . House House isn't alone in taking this action. Narrative platformer Celeste and party fighter TowerFall have delisted from Xbox recently, and Maddy Thorson of Maddy Makes Games fame took to BlueSky to explain why: "For those who’re asking, yes, we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox. We did this to support the BDS boycott." For reference, Microsoft gets a cut whenever it makes a sale through its proprietary digital distribution storefront, similar to Steam. Console producers tend to take a loss on hardware, subsidizing it for accessibility to more consumers, so they can make up the difference by selling other stuff, a crucial slice of that other stuff being games. So as long as sales trickle in for critically acclaimed games like Celeste and TowerFall, that's a bit of easy money for Microsoft—the choice to delist the game stops that. If you're an Xbox owner who wants to observe the boycott, you can always buy used physical versions of games where that's an option or switch to another platform for the time being. But this is PC Gamer dot com, so you probably haven't even heard of the Xbox. You've certainly never seen one up close. sources.title: Bungie Says 'Don't Buy Marathon as a Donation' as Destiny Players Look to Support Studio's Future
sources.text: As Bungie plots a future for more Destiny , head of product Josh Deane has clarified that players don't need to "buy Marathon as a donation" just to support the studio's plans. It's a clarification that arrived after Deane posted a community message for Destiny fans yesterday. The message, featured as part of a lengthy Q&A blog post , outlined the unvaulting process for Destiny 2 content that was previously promised last month, but one segment left players confused – and concerned – about the future and extraction shooter Marathon's role in the big picture. "We're not going to forget the mistakes of the past, but it's time to learn from them and unify as one Bungie community," the section in question said. "For us, the majority of our Bungie team is legacy Destiny, and we will all tell you that nothing can help bridge us into future more than for Marathon to rapidly evolve and become sustainable. As we head into our December and March updates for Marathon, it’s a formative period for all of us here at Bungie that will help determine the shape of our future, so please encourage each other and know that your support gives our team the energy to finish the fight." It's the "nothing can help us bridge us into future more than for Marathon to rapidly evolve and become sustainable" bit that's got the Destiny community so riled up. With the back-and-forth pulling Destiny 2 in and out of the fire all through the span of a few months, some believed Bungie was trying to tell its audience that picking up a copy of its new sci-fi FPS would help keep it and the studio's future secure. Deane stepped in to confirm this is not the case. The Bungie developer said his intention was not to rest the Destiny revival on the shoulders of the fans that helped breathe life back into it earlier this year. He chalks it up to a mistranslation, "and that's on me." "In no way is the Destiny plan contingent upon Marathon," Deane added. "Play what inspires you, whatever it is. Mainly hoping we can accomplish our goals in both lanes with a stronger relationship with our entire community!" I may have worded this clumsily but this is the true heart of what I was trying to say Truly care about community healing and believe that it will help our studio bridge into the future in the most healthy way possible ❤️ Play and share what you are passionate about, whatever that is The Destiny plan moves forward no matter what When one player suggested they feared they were being encouraged to purchase but never download Marathon just to support Bungie, Deane said , "Oh, don't buy Marathon as a donation or offer anything else." "It's our job to show up for you," he added. When another fan expressed similar concern, he said , "I truly love the sentiment but only buy or play a thing that inspires you from us / you think is cool! We will find our way back home with Destiny." So, there you have it: Destiny and Marathon don't depend upon the success of the other. As Bungie principal comms manager Dylan Gafner said , "Two cakes! One big community." That should offer some relief not only to Destiny players who feared their favorite game's future may still be in jeopardy but also to Marathon players who have feared the same. Negativity has surrounded both games in recent months, with community members on each side going at each other as both struggled. For now, we know that the Destiny franchise will live on with a few projects. These include "celebration" content updates, a project that the team has teased as "Destiny 'Legacy'," and a mysterious "redacted" project. For Marathon, Bungie will continue to try to revitalize the extraction shooter with Symbiosis this December. The studio also recently reassured players that the extraction component is "still a major part" of the experience as the team experiments with PvE and Deathmatch modes. What's next for Destiny and Marathon remains to be seen, but it's clear Bungie is putting in the work to keep both afloat. While we wait to see how things pan out, you can see why the studio believes the latter struggled at launch . You can also read about how the Destiny community banded together to help the #SaveMassEffect movement . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

sources.title: John Romero confirms his axed Xbox game has a new publisher and he’s rehired some staff
sources.text: The game has been rescoped for a smaller team and “we’re just super happy”, he says Doom and Quake co-creator and id Software co-founder John Romero says his unannounced shooter project, which was dropped by Xbox earlier this year, now has a new publisher. This summer, Romero Games confirmed it had lost funding for the unannounced shooter project, after an unspecified publisher, later named as Microsoft , pulled its publishing agreement as part of a wave of layoffs across the corporation. Multiple employees claimed the âwhole studioâ was let go as a result of the pulled publishing deal, though Romero Games later denied it was closing and said it still hoped another publisher could save the project. Now, speaking to VGC today during Gamescom Asia, Romero has confirmed that the game has a new publisher and some of the staff previously working on it have been rehired. “You know, last year we basically got defunded, like a lot of people did,” Romero told us, “and so we had to spend time figuring out what we were going to do. “Eventually we decided that we canât keep everybody on forever, and we kept them on as long as we could, trying to find funding to finish the game, keep everybody there, but as time goes on and people leave you canât build that game again. “So at some point we were like âokay, we canât do that, so we need to do redundancy and then figure out what weâre going to do with a super-small team’. We were 110 people, going down to five. “So we went down to five people, we had this big game that we had made. We 100% own everything. We own the name, we own all the IP, all the art, all the graphics, the code and everything. And so I needed to basically design a new game that could use as much of that stuff as possible, to just basically get a head start. “I just contacted somebody that I knew, and we basically did a deal, and so we have a new publisher. Can’t say anything about who it is, or when the announce is, or any of that stuff.” Romero told us the studio has “brought 10 people back”, who were “the leads of the different sub-teams that we had”, but stressed that the current team size of around 15-16 staff was likely where it would stay for now, with the game being redesigned and rescaled accordingly. “We don’t need to be bigger than that, the game is scoped for a team that’s that size and we’re just super happy,” he explained. “The gameâs going extremely well, weâre very happy with it. “I mean, itâs a shooter â that part totally makes sense â but everything else around it is really new, and everybody on the team is so excited. Weâre very excited with how the game is turning out.” Speaking about the game originally planned, Romero said: “Weâre not getting that game to the end. That game we canât get to the end, because itâs a 110-person game. So this is a complete redesign of a totally different game, but it uses a lot of the work that we had in the previous games. So itâs like âhereâs all these characters that we can move overâ, you know? âArt, code assets â I mean, shooters have a lot of common code â so weâve moved a bunch of stuff over to the new game, which got us a big head-start, starting with really great art, cool weapons, all that kind of stuff. So itâs one thing to finish a 110-person game, [but] with that small of a team it canât really happen â the complexity is too much. We had that team size because we needed that team size.â “I mean, itâs a shooter â that part totally makes sense â but everything else around it is really new, and everybody on the team is so excited. Weâre very excited with how the game is turning out.” Romero said he preferred working with a smaller team because it allows him to be more involved the day-to-day making of the game too, instead of trying to manage various departments. “Iâve had teams of that size [100+ staff] before, but I donât like it when Iâm just in meetings all day,” he told us. “I like to make the game, designing by hand, and thatâs whatâs happening right now â making every single decision, working in Unreal Editor, making stuff, designing things, directing all the rest of the people on the team. “It’s a small team, and the people are self-driven because they’re all leads. They know what to do. They all know what the game is. They get the whole thing. We work very closely because it’s pretty much flat.” Asked whether he’d ever like to work with a large publisher again, Romero told us: “No. Because I really like to be in the game. “I donât like having a bunch of producers, because a bunch of producers means a bunch of people, and right now thereâs no producer. Itâs great. Donât need it, weâre all leads, we know how it goes, it’s not complex. So, we’re at the right size. We don’t need a producer yet, and we’re not going to get one. So, yeah, I guess as soon as you need a producer, you’re too big. “As far as I’m concerned, I love small teams, and it’s way more fun making games on small teams. You can pivot â in hours you can completely pivot everything if you have to. “It’s also the deal that we haveâ¦ every publisher has various things that they put in the contract. And most of the time you’re working with the publisher to make the game that they believe will make money, and that your vision is going to hopefully meet at the same point of making money. “A lot of times the publisher changes what your game is going to be because they have a specialization, or they know something you don’t, and they want to steer you in a certain direction because of whoever they are. “The publisher weâre with right now has zero creative goals for this game. Theyâre like âyou make what you want, weâre publishing it, weâre not going to tell you what to makeâ. Thatâs the perfect deal, you know?”

sources.text: "We don't need to be bigger than that, the game is scoped for a team that's that size and we're just super happy" id Software co-founder John Romero says that his studio's axed Xbox title has a new publisher, with a smaller staff reworking the game's scope. Romero Games announced that it was working on an "all-new FPS with an original, new IP" back in 2022. But in the summer of 2025, in the wake of what has become yearly layoffs at Xbox, the project was seemingly cancelled . It became clear after the announcement that the game's unannounced publisher had been Xbox, and Romero Games was put at risk of shutdown in the wake of more Microsoft cuts. Now, over a year later, Romero has updated VGC on the studio's current standing. He says that the studio kept on staff "as long as we could, trying to find funding to finish the game." But eventually, the studio was forced to "do redundancy and then figure out what we're going to do with a super-small team." The team of 110 people went down to five at one point, but Romero says that the FPS title has a new publisher, and that the studio has "brought 10 people back." The returning devs were "the leads of the different sub-teams that we had." The game is being redesigned in accordance with the smaller team. "We don't need to be bigger than that, the game is scoped for a team that's that size and we're just super happy," Romero explains. As far as the original plans, he says, "We're not getting that game to the end. That game we can't get to the end, because it's a 110-person game. So this is a complete redesign of a totally different game, but it uses a lot of the work that we had in the previous games." However, Romero notes "we've moved a bunch of stuff over to the new game, which got us a big head-start, starting with really great art, cool weapons, all that kind of stuff." As for the new publisher, Romero notes that he's unable to reveal what it is, but notes it's pretty hands off. "The publisher we're with right now has zero creative goals for this game. They're like 'you make what you want, we're publishing it, we're not going to tell you what to make'. That's the perfect deal, you know?" stories.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove footage of real-life Seoul crush
stories.summary: The bereaved families said "using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless"

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove footage of real-life Seoul crush
sources.text: The bereaved families said "using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless" Activision has confirmed that it will be removing real-life news footage of the 2022 crush in Itaewon from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 following backlash. On October 29, 2022, a crowd crush happened in the Itaewon neighborhood of Seoul, South Korea during Halloween festivities which drew over 100,000 people to the area. This crush resulted in the deaths of 160 people, and a further 196 people were injured during the event marking one of the deadliest disasters in the country's history. Almost exactly four years on from the incident, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has caused controversy by including a video of rescue efforts following the event as part of an in-universe news report at the end of the game's first mission. The footage contains people performing CPR, bodybags lining the streets and people being wheeled on a stretcher. The bereaved families issued a statement earlier this week (via BBC News ), saying, "We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used as it was to create a scene in a game." It adds, "Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless," and continues, "If the game developer has even a minimum of courtesy and empathy towards the victims, it should take corrective action without delay." In a statement to BBC News , Activision confirms the use of the real-life footage, saying it was used "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insists that the inclusion was "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form." Activision offers condolences to the families and victims of the incident and confirms the footage will be removed from Modern Warfare 4. Activision and Infinity Ward have previously caused controversy by referencing real-life events in their games. 2019's Modern Warfare reboot was accused of attempting to rewrite history after having the US-led attacks on a highway between Kuwait and Iraq in 1991, dubbed the Highway of Death – which is the name it is referenced by in-game – mentioned as a Russian attack. The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association told the BBC that the group welcomed Activision's decision, but that the publisher has not reached out with a direct apology. sources.title: Activision apologizes and says it will remove South Korean crush footage from Modern Warfare 4 after victims’ families speak out
sources.text: A shot in the game’s intro shows news footage from the site of the tragedy Activision has apologised to those offended by its use of footage from a real-life tragedy in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and pledges to remove it. The game, which mainly focuses on conflict between North Korea and South Korea, has an opening title sequence featuring a montage of news reports discussing the gameâs fictional outbreak of a full-scale North Korean invasion into the South Korean mainland. The newsreaderâs voiceovers are accompanied by archival clips taken from actual news reports, including a brief shot of a paramedic giving CPR to someone lying on the floor. Players identified this shot as news footage from the aftermath of the 2022 Halloween crowd crush tragedy in Itaewon, Seoul, in which a crowd surge in a narrow alleyway during a heavily populated street party led to 159 deaths and 196 injuries. This led to statements from the October 29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and the Korea Game Users Association, who both called on Activision to remove the footage. Now South Korean publication Inven reports that Activision has apologised for the use of the footage, and says it will be removed from the game as part of its next update, which is scheduled for November 12. In a statement distributed to South Korean media, Activision said (as translated by Inven): “ Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a work of fiction created to provide realistic immersion. We make it clear that in using actual news broadcast footage within the game, we never intended to evoke or trivialize any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush.” “The video footage in question will be completely removed through a game update scheduled for distribution on November 12. We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims who were deeply hurt by this incident, as well as to everyone we have caused concern.”

sources.title: Ubisoft não tem nenhum remake de Assassin’s Creed em desenvolvimento atualmente
sources.text: Apesar da boa recepção de Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced , a Ubisoft confirmou que não possui outros remakes da franquia em desenvolvimento atualmente. Em atualização publicada na última quinta (29), a empresa comentou o aprendizado com o projeto e explicou que suas equipes estão concentradas nos próximos capítulos da série. A desenvolvedora também destacou que o sucesso de Resynced mostrou o interesse dos jogadores em revisitar aventuras clássicas. No entanto, a possibilidade de novos remakes não foi descartada — já que a Ubisoft pretende continuar avaliando oportunidades para trazer alguns clássicos de volta. A Ubisoft afirmou que desenvolver Black Flag Resynced foi uma experiência importante para entender os desafios de reconstruir um jogo querido pelos fãs. O trabalho envolveu refazer sistemas antigos, adicionar novos elementos e equilibrar as mudanças com a identidade da aventura original. “Reconstruir sistemas antigos do zero, adicionar novos elementos que se encaixam na experiência e equilibrar o legado com a inovação foi uma tarefa gigantesca”, explicou a gigante francesa. A desenvolvedora também declarou estar orgulhosa do resultado entregue pela equipe responsável pelo projeto. Apesar da recepção positiva, a Ubisoft foi direta ao esclarecer que não há outro remake de Assassin’s Creed em produção neste momento. “Nossas equipes já estão focadas no próximo capítulo da franquia Assassin’s Creed , incluindo projetos que vocês ainda não conhecem, com novos cenários e histórias”, afirmou. Isso não significa, porém, que a empresa tenha abandonado a ideia de revisitar outros títulos. A Ubisoft declarou que gosta da possibilidade de recuperar aventuras antigas e continuará avaliando oportunidades para desenvolver novos remakes no futuro. A franquia também passa por uma reorganização de sua liderança. Liderada por Martin Schelling, a nova equipe responsável por Assassin’s Creed trabalha na definição das prioridades e da visão de longo prazo para os próximos anos da série. Entre os objetivos apresentados pela Ubisoft estão preservar a identidade da franquia, continuar inovando, oferecer experiências variadas e melhorar a qualidade e a consistência dos lançamentos. A empresa também pretende manter uma narrativa mais coesa e respeitar os elementos que definem o universo da série. A desenvolvedora afirmou que milhares de jogadores participaram de uma pesquisa comunitária realizada em março. Entre os principais pontos levantados estavam a preservação dos pilares da franquia, o desenvolvimento de histórias mais conectadas e a necessidade de uma comunicação mais frequente com os fãs. Para ampliar esse diálogo, a Ubisoft planeja realizar workshops fechados com integrantes da comunidade e criadores de conteúdo. Uma nova pesquisa também foi disponibilizada, enquanto a empresa incentiva os jogadores a acompanharem as oportunidades de participação pelo Discord oficial. Além dos projetos ainda não anunciados, a Ubisoft atualizou o andamento de dois jogos conhecidos da comunidade: Codename Invictus e Codename Hexe . Ambos continuam em desenvolvimento, mas seguem propostas diferentes dentro do universo de Assassin’s Creed . Invictus é um projeto multiplayer competitivo que passou por uma primeira sessão privada de testes com centenas de jogadores. Segundo a Ubisoft, o retorno foi positivo em relação ao parkour, à verticalidade dos mapas e ao trabalho em equipe, mas a equipe também recebeu pedidos para reforçar elementos tradicionais da franquia. Já o Codename Hexe promete uma experiência mais sombria dentro da série e continua em desenvolvimento. A empresa afirmou que ainda há trabalho pela frente e que pretende compartilhar uma nova atualização mais significativa sobre o projeto em 2027. A Ubisoft também reforçou que Black Flag Resynced recebeu sua última grande atualização recentemente , enquanto as equipes seguem trabalhando nos próximos projetos da saga de assassinos templários. sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Xbox's Doom, Wolfenstein Developers Working 'More Closely Than Ever' Following Xbox 'Reset' Layoffs
sources.text: Bethesda and Xbox development studio id Software, maker of the Doom franchise, has deepened its partnership with fellow Bethesda and Xbox studio MachineGames, makers of the most recent Wolfenstein games as well as 2024's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. At a press event earlier this week for id Software's Doom: The Dark Ages - Revelations DLC, which was released this summer, studio co-director Marty Stratton was asked how the studio is doing in the wake of the layoffs that affected id as part of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's ongoing Xbox " reset ." He answered, "We're doing great. Not to handwave the [layoffs] away...everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that. But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department. "We're working more closely with MachineGames than ever. We've always had a very close partnership with them, but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]. We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead." This is purely speculative on my part, but might the two decorated first-person shooter studios be co-developing MachineGames's next project, which is heavily rumored to be Wolfenstein 3 – with studio head Jerk Gustafsson saying, "We're not done with Wolfenstein yet"? Not only has MachineGames used id Software's idTech engine for every one of its games, but Sharma has publicly stated that she wants Xbox's development teams to double down on their biggest franchises – a sentiment echoed by Bethesda boss Jill Braff. And with id now seemingly done with Doom: The Dark Ages following the oustanding Revelations DLC, a team-up with MachineGames might help get the rumored third Wolfenstein game out the door faster, and getting games out more quickly is one of Sharma's goals. In addition, while Doom should certainly be considered in that "biggest franchises" group, Wolfenstein most likely is as well. Plus, Amazon has a Wolfenstein TV series in development, which might further incentivize Xbox and Bethesda to pair up id and MachineGames to make sure the latter team's next game is as awesome – and out as quickly – as possible. Bu whatever either team does next, the project(s) will be highly anticipated, at least by me, as both teams have incredible track records, both historically and recently. Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

sources.title: A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion
sources.text: A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project. The unofficial project , which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind. Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025. In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work. A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked. According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate". The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch. Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named. "Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion". Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026 .

sources.title: Fan-made Oblivion remake Skyblivion runs into legal trouble with a former volunteer
sources.text: "A 'take your ball and go home' approach like this fundamentally contradicts the collaborative, open spirit of the modding community" Skyblivion (the fan-made Oblivion remake that's being rebuilt inside of Skyrim) has been a long time coming, but we might need to wait a while longer for the conversion mod to see the light of day due to a new legal issue. One of the ambitious project's lead modders, Rebelzize, today uploaded a video about the ongoing situation. "Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion's development departed the project. We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure," he explains in the description. "After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked," Rebelzize adds. Rebelzize doesn't name the former modder in an effort to avoid creating an online "witch hunt," but they eventually sent the Skyblivion folks a series of legal threats demanding the real names and home addresses of several other volunteer team members - "something that we are simply not willing to share with somebody that we don't even know," Rebelzize says, calling the demands "disproportionate." The former modder is apparently looking to sue for damages worth upwards of €30,000. "A 'take your ball and go home' approach like this fundamentally contradicts the collaborative, open spirit of the modding community that makes massive passion projects like this possible," Rebelzize continues. "To protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break, in good faith we removed their code, rebuilding and improving the system from the ground up." Despite removing their work from Skyblivion, the anonymous former volunteer has apparently "continued to intensify their threats." The Skyblivion team is now looking for help from anyone experienced in IP and GDPR law, pointing interested folks toward their official website . Last year, it looked like a Skyblivion release date could be right around the corner . There's still no word on when we can expect the gorgeous fan-led revival, though. sources.title: Nintendo Reveals Surprise Pikmin Day Direct
sources.text: Nintendo has revealed a surprise Nintendo Direct for Pikmin Day because it has apparently decided that's a thing now. Instead of spooky game announcements or horror movie memes, video game fans woke up to on Halloween 2026 was Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto's face. That's because Nintendo has declared November 1 as Pikmin Day, and it's got a brand-new Direct to celebrate the occasion. Yes, really. None of this is a joke. There's a little more than nine minutes of announcements to go over. Although there's no Pikmin 5 reveal or anything else too groundbreaking here, Miyamoto did take the time to share new information about Pikmin 4 and promised that, "going forward, I want people to know more about Pikmin." Tomorrow is Pikmin Day! Join in on the fun by playing Pikmin games on Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch. https://t.co/iYxZldya7p So, to start, why is the first of November Pikmin Day? Nintendo's miniaturized franchise launched in Japan in October 2001 before coming to North America in December, so there's no tie to a release date like you might have guessed. Instead, Miyamoto explained that November 1 is Pikmin Day because there were originally only three Pikmin, which, when standing next to each other, kinda looks like "11.1." Ready to test your skills at Dandori Academy? A free demo of #Pikmin4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy will be available on Nov 2. https://t.co/rNHNq35RMT You gotta give 'em credit for creativity, as Pikmin Day is probably one of the last things anyone expected to see today. Still, it served as a nice opportunity to offer an update on Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy ahead of its release November 12, 2026. Players will be able to use the new consoles built-in microphone to Oatchi, controlling them by using commands like 'rush' and 'go to work.' The Dandori Academy mode, meanwhile, comes with new challenges, including exams that take place on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, that give players timed tasks and an opportunity to earn medals. A demo for the Switch 2 version of Pikimin 4 will be available starting November 2, with save data available to transfer to the full launch. It offers access to the Sun-Speckled Terrace opening area, as well as two Dandori Academy stages. Secret Caves are coming this winter! Get ready to explore Secret Caves, face off against familiar creatures, and uncover hidden treasures along the way in @PikminBloom on your smartphone. https://t.co/Nx6Lzba6v4 Nintendo first brought its augmented-reality game, Pikmin Bloom, to smartphone devices in 2021, but five years on, and it's still got more to give. As shown in a teaser video featuring a group of the colorful plant-like creatures battling a Bulborb, an update scheduled to arrive this winter will add a new mechanic called Secret Caves. These battle-focused exploration events allow players to take their crew into caves to battle creatures and earn rewards. Before a cave is explored, players must collect a cave map, which feature information about a cave and can be found on things like Postcards. Then, Pikmin are sent into the cave to search for treasures, with some of the items highlighted during the Direct including a rubber duck, a sword, a cookie, and a chef hat. Should a battle ensue, you'll command your army by sending them in to attack when the moment is right, or retreat if things get too hairy. Pikmin 4's Dandori Academy challenges also give players an opportunity to collect maps by taking exams. If you couldn't tell from the video games, shorts , and Easter Eggs Nintendo has highlighted through the franchise's 25-year history, it's got a soft spot for Pikmin. Miyamoto has spearheaded this charge, and because he wants people to know more about the company's adorable little mascots, he's enlisted some help. Joining him during the Nintendo Direct broadcast was Japanese actress and crafty Pikmin fan Fuka Koshiba. Known for her work on TV projects like Siren and films like Lady Kaga, Miyamoto brought her in to help him "build more excitement around Pikmin going forward" after she shared hand-made Pikmin-themed hats on Instagram. "Originally, I had heard on social media that you could get hats of the Red Pikmin, Blue Pikmin, and Yellow Pikmin from those claw machines," Koshiba said, holding one of her hats. "I'm not good at the claw machines, but I really wanted the hats, so I thought, 'Well, let's just knit them.'" "I see," Miyamoto replied. "I'm also bad at the claw machines." That was a close one! Watch Hello! Pikmin short movies and enjoy new Pikmin adventures. https://t.co/8OPB48hDZr The Pikmin Day Direct also featured a brand-new Pikmin Original Short Movie. Following last year's Close to You short, this video sees a Red Pikmin do its best to grab a baseball from a frog. It's as cute as you could ever expect. As part of Nintendo's initiative to lean harder into the series, new shorts will be released monthly via the Nintendo Today! app, as well as other channels. However, there will also be a new episode released tomorrow, with another set to follow sometime in November. Miyamoto said he's collaborating with Nintendo Pictures staff to make the shorts. That's all for the Pikmin Day Direct. While there was no hint at anything like Pikmin 5, planting November 1 as an official holiday is probably a sign that Nintendo has no intention of putting a cap on Pikmin content anytime soon. While we wait for any bigger updates on the franchise, you can check out IGN's 9/10 Pikmin 4 review . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

sources.text: November is typically a major month for video game releases, and 2026 is no exception. The biggest game of the month is undoubtedly Grand Theft Auto 6 , which is one of the most anticipated entertainment events of all time. But Rockstar’s magnum opus isn’t coming to Switch 2 — not yet, anyway. That said, there are still plenty of intriguing new games coming out for Nintendo’s hybrid console in November. Here are five that we’re especially excited about. November’s biggest Switch 2 release just happens to be a console exclusive — and it’s the perfect contrast to all the lurid excess of GTA 6 . The Nintendo 64 classic revolutionized 3D game designed with its player-controlled camera, lock-on combat, and contextual controls. This top-down remake ditches the original's low-poly asethetic for a sumptuous toyland art style and modernized controls. After a 30-minute hands-on preview in October, Polygon’s Michael McWhertor came away thoroughly impressed. “One impression of the remake remained consistent throughout my hands-on time: Nintendo’s new Zelda is snappy, streamlined, and polished in ways that make it feel totally fresh,” he wrote. 2020’s Marvel’s Avengers cast a long and unflattering shadow, owing to its tedious endgame loop and aggressive live-service monetization. But Eidos-Montréal’s Guardians of the Galaxy is something altogether different. This single-player action-adventure game balances spectacle with heartfelt moments — and it has a killer soundtrack bursting with ‘80s bangers. Ensemble casts can often feel a little too yappy, but the banter here is genuinely funny and doesn’t grow tiresome. Guardians was nominated for four Game Awards and ultimately took home the prize for Best Narrative. The Encore Edition is exclusive to Switch 2 and includes a new set of glam rock outfits for Star-Lord, Drax, Gamora, Rocket and Groot. Put aside the exhausting internet discourse surrounding Stellar Blade ’s protagonist Eve, and you’re left with a rock-solid action game that will put your countering and parrying skills to the test. As Eve, you’re tasked with reclaiming Earth from a hostile alien species, and along the way you’ll piece together the dramatic events that lead to the fall of civilization. Though the customization and skill tree leave a bit to be desired compared to similar character action games, the exhilarating combat and roller-coaster final act make for a memorable 20-25-hour experience. This acclaimed 2023 RPG takes Atlus’s trademark combo of dungeon crawling and social sim elements from the Persona series and applies it to an entirely new world. Instead of a Japanese high school, Metaphor takes place in a medieval fantasy realm after the assassination of its King. In order to determine his successor, aspiring rulers must compete in a Royal Tournament and rally support from people throughout the nation. With an endearing ensemble cast, bonkers enemy designs, and some fantastically devious dungeons, this 80-hour epic will keep you entertained throughout the crisp autumn days. There’s a demo available now in the Nintendo eShop and your progress will carry over to the full game. Nintendo’s chill real-time strategy game from 2023 is getting a Switch 2 glow-up. Despite some occasional hitches with combat and excessive pop-up suggestions, Pikmin 4 is a deeply optimistic and cheerful experience. In Polygon’s review from July 2023, Emily Price noted, “ Pikmin 4 accomplishes maybe the best thing a piece of media can do — it makes the real world seem more wondrous than it did before.” The Switch 2 version features enhanced visuals, the ability to issue voice commands to your dog friend Oatchi, and the Dandori Academy treasure-collection challenge mode.

stories.title: Persona 1 Remake Footage Seemingly Leaks Online

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Persona 1 Remake Footage Seemingly Leaks Online
sources.text: What appears to be gameplay footage from an unannounced Persona 1 remake has leaked online. A little less than two minutes of video depicting what looks a lot like a modern version of Sega and Atlus' original Persona game was first published on Reddit before being spread around various social media platforms today. The developers behind the RPG franchise have broached the topic of remakes for early installments in the past but never confirmed work was underway, meaning this could be our first look at the series' next remake. The original post says the footage is tied to a Persona: Be Your True Mind remake. In the age of AI-generated fakes, you can never be too skeptical about things like this, but fans generally seem to be under the impression that the footage is authentic. We won't share it here, but you don't have to look too hard on places like X/Twitter or YouTube to see what everyone's talking about. Yea that Persona 1 remake leaked footage gotta be 100% real. I refuse to believe someone would do that much work to make a fake leak. There are a few reasons players suspect this to be our first glimpse at a not-so-secret Persona 1 remake from Atlus. Aside from the music, effects, and art, which all fall right in line with much of the studio's recent work, the video on display is much longer and more detailed than any fake leak would typically be. The smoking gun for many, though, is the character animations. It's specifically Eriko that people are calling out, as she seems to share a summoning animation with Persona 4 Revival 's version of Yukiko. Atlus' Persona 4 remake, of course, won't be out until February 18, 2027. There's also the issue of the appearance of Persona 2 protagonist Tatsuya, who seems to be standing in for what may be an unfinished character model. So, what can we make of all of this? Well, unfortunately, without confirmation from Sega or Atlus, not much. There is always the chance this could be an elaborate fake, with some of these odd details serving as evidence for that argument. On the other hand, it's possible placeholder assets and familiar animations are here specifically because the alleged Persona 1 remake is still very much in development. Persona 1 leak looks credible, not sure why people are reporting Tatsuya is replacing Masao, that's just complete bogus. This is most likely an internal investor pitch for remakes of Persona 1 and 2, and not actually Persona 1. There are Persona 4 Revival animations in the gameplay footage, which definitely helps the case of it being real. That sure is a persona 1 remake trailer. Why is tatsuya there We don't know when this footage would have been captured, even if it does turn out to be real. That means this could be from yesterday or years ago, with some speculating that the video we've seen today is little more than a proof-of-concept or pitch video. If the Persona: Be Your True Mind remake footage is authentic, it wouldn't be the biggest surprise to see it announced. Sega released its Persona 3 remake, Persona 3 Reload , in 2024, and will release Persona 4 Revival in just a few months. Atlus' P-Studio producer, Kazuhisa Wada, stopped short of confirming development for Persona 1 and 2 remakes in August of this year but still admitted that, as far as he's concerned, it's something "we have to do." Meanwhile, Atlus has absolutely suffered leaks before. The Persona 3 remake had in-development footage questioned by fans when it showed up online back in 2023. sources.title: Anthropic Blocks AI Game Clones in Claude Opus Update
sources.text: Anthropic has issued an update for Claude that puts a stop to the AI-generated game clones that have filled platforms like Steam. The term 'AI slop' is something we've heard a lot in the past few years, but it became especially prevalent in the gaming community after Valve launched Steam Next Fest earlier this month. PC users quickly launched complaints that their feeds had been filled with low-effort clones not only of pre-existing games but even some titles that had only just released their own demos. As players trudged through the slop, developers faced a reality that threw months or even years of hard work into jeopardy. Some, including Drunken Goddess Reflux developer Alliance Arts and Who You , even took action by canceling their Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. It's a situation that rapidly spun out of control, prompting a response from Valve itself as it said it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem." ANTHROPIC IS CRACKING DOWN ON VIDEO GAME REWRITES 🚨 Claude Code picked up a new rule around Oct 27, sent from Anthropic’s servers under a flag called "tengu_heron_brook". There’s no setting to turn it off. The full rule: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.” Is this the end of game rewrites, modding and everything in between? As reported by Game Developer , X/Twitter user Chasm was one of the first to share evidence of tech company Anthropic taking action against video game copycats. Based on their findings, Claude, the company's AI assistant, recently received an update featuring a new rule. The full rule can be read below: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." When reached for comment by Game Developer, Anthropic pointed to a post shared by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff. Osmani's explanation can be read below: "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Whether there was a specific event or reason that prompted Anthropic to make these changes is unclear. Game developers and game enjoyers will no doubt find comfort in Anthropic's changes, though it's worth noting that how impactful any of this will be remains to be seen. At the very least, those who use Claude to rip ideas directly from those who used their minds and time to bring them to life should have a tougher time trying to profit off of the work of others. The industry is struggling to come to grips with artificial intelligence. Some, such as Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, have insisted that Valve should stray from asking developers to disclose games utilizing generative AI materials . Others, including Super Smash Bros. mastermind Masahiro Sakurai, have compared AI-generated games to "low-quality goods." The developers behind VRChat, meanwhile, recently came under fire for how they are handling AI content . Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN.
